The Big Battle Theory: Why Combat Is Required For An RPG

Combat isn't necessary in an RPG, the author is just trying desperately to hold on to the nostalgia of his childhood. "Role Playing Game" Look at the words. An RPG is a game which let's you play a role. There is no reason to expect that to mean "A game which lets you kill things". Look at the Fallout series, in multiple titles, combat is left as completely optional, although the games are geared towards being combat-heavy, if a player chooses not to harm anything does that make the game less of an RPG? Of course not.

The example the author uses most heavily is "To the Moon", claiming that it isn't a true RPG because it doesn't allow combat. I haven't played To the Moon, but I don't see how removing combat from a game stops it from being an RPG. The author claims that combat is a space for player's to emotionally bond with NPCs. I disagree completely. Going back to Fallout, in NV, resolving Cass's story peacefully gave me an incredibly accomplished feeling, curbing a character who was filled with anger to let go and move on without violence made me feel more connected to her than senselessly slaughtering any number of Van Graffs.

The best quests in any series are the non-violent ones, because they're the most real. Game violence is fun and has it's place in certain RPGs, especially fantasy titles which want you to feel powerful, but sometimes violence and power isn't what an RPG needs, sometimes it needs soul.

The problem i see with "an rpg is any game where you play a role" is that then every game is a role playing game. Call of duty, you play the role of a soldier. Star craft, you play the role of a future commander. Tomb raider, you play the role of laura croft. But i think we would all agree that these arnt RPGs.

To me he's partially correct in that what makes it an RPG is stats and dice rolls. However, unlike what he said, you don't need combat to have stats and dice rolls. I spent more time rolling dice in non-combat situations playing D and D then i did in fights. And i frequently put points in skills that only helped out side of fighting. You can absolutely have a non-combat rpg. As someone who had played "to the moon" i do agree that its not a RPG, it's an adventure game. There are no stats, there are no dice rolls.

So do you need combat to have an rpg? No. Do you need stats and dice rolls to have an rpg? Absolutely.

Hah. It is fascinating how much RPG elements have saturated other genres. Seems everything triple A bolts on some sort of XP system. Maybe some sort of inventory screen. Collectible weapons, random drops. All the skinner box elements of RPGs that speak to our more compulsive nature, and which many people think are downright exploitative.

It is hard to pinpoint what the heart and soul of what a "true" RPG is, if there is such a thing.

You are spot-on that the "role" argument turns RPG into a useless term. If everything is an RPG, then nothing is an RPG.

I do think that in videogames RPGs have neglected the noncombatant roles and manners of play, but that for a long time has been the nature of the beast for video game RPGs. Imagine for a moment a quest for you to heal a sick person, with the antidote being held by a wicked beast deep in a monster-filled cave. In a videogame setting usually that is it. You must delve into that cave, defeat the beast, collect the cure, and return to complete the quest. There are no other options because all solutions have to be preprogrammed into the game. In a tabletop environment, a stealthy character could attempt to slip past all of the creatures and steal the cure, or certain industrious characters could say "a cave full of bloodthirsty beasts? Forget that noise," with the player making a couple stat and skill checks to produce the cure themselves. That's possible because the DM/GM is there to make sure that any and all possibilities are left open to the characters, as long as they are within the rules and the dice favor them. They can still award XP for dealing with the situation, even if it wasn't via the expected route.

So... what do I really think makes a roleplaying game?

Stats, skills, and dice rolls - absolutely, they are the mechanism granting options and chance. Combat - not necessarily, but the combatant role is a role and should be an option. XP, Levels, skill/stat increases - absolutely, growth within your chosen role to increase options should be available.

So, really, the common theme is "options" : the ability to play the role you choose for yourself. Eliminating combat entirely and turning the game into a visual novel does not suit that purpose any more than focusing solely on combat and turning the game into an action title.

I think there has been some effort to accommodate different roles in some major titles. Skyrim would be a notable one. However, in those titles, there often is still a combat-based bottleneck to quest solutions. Of course for some quests this makes sense. An evil demon ravaging a city isn't going to stop its pillaging because a thief stealthily snuck past it, or because a merchant with high speechcraft skill gave it a stern talking to (even if you roll a natural 20). However, I think creative options could be given allowing those characters to defeat the demon in their own way. Perhaps a demon-banishing relic could exist in another town, curated by a priest. The silver-tongued merchant could attempt to acquire it with a substantial donation to the church, or the thief could attempt to steal it. In any event, the XP reward for killing the demon in combat or for banishing it with the relic should be equal, not treated as a redheaded stepchild sort of solution.

I don't believe giving those kinds of options would harm the RPG genre. I think it would be bringing it closer to its tabletop heritage. Though I do understand the challenges that poses to developers... I don't think it's a challenge which they cannot meet.

I hear this repeatedly. Sometimes I wonder how much of this is revisionist history. I was too young to be involved in the earliest versions of D&D. But all the earliest pen & paper RPGs I played in middle school and high school in the 90's were very combat and stat focused. A lot of that could have been our lack of imagination, or it could have been the fact that we were nerds with more affinity for numbers and math than fabricating rich internal inner thoughts for imaginary people. I don't know how common this was, but I'm pretty sure it wasn't uncommon. Especially from what I know about RPGs having gotten their start in the numbers heavy world of conflict simulators or wargames.

Now it's true you see a lot of indie RPGs with more emphasis on acting and being social, and no combat or statistics at all. But this is a decidedly modern invention, and I have a hard time imagining anybody I knew who was into RPGs in the 90's having any interest in a system that didn't provide plenty of numbers of obsess over and no combat.

I didn't say "no combat", only that it should not be used as the only solution to all problems.

I've been playing tabletop RPGs since the 80s, and certainly I've been in combat-heavy groups, but even in those groups combat wasn't presented as the only solution.

A quickie example:
Party is tasked with stopping an evil cult from awakening an ancient demon. Party reaches the site of the cult ritual. Several dozen cultists are gathered around an altar where the high-priest is performing the blood ritual.
Okay, the obvious solution is to kill all of the cultists then kill the priest before he can complete the ritual, and the GM let us know (via knowledge check success on our mage) that we had little time left.
One of our... slower (to put it kindly), players asked, "Well, can't we just f--- up the altar from here?"
Some more knowledge checks and a little creative strategizing later, and we launched a long-range assault against the tools of the ritual, instead of slogging through the cultists on a murder-spree, and we were dying laughing as we escaped unscathed.
The GM later told us there was basically no way we could have killed the priest in time, he had every intention of making us fight the demon, most likely killing a few of us in the process, but we "dumbstumbled" on a solution he hadn't considered when writing the scenario.
Did that solution deserve less reward than the murder-spree solution?

Like I said though, I love combat too. I had great fun method-acting a drunken master in an AD&D campaign with my fist-based diplomacy, often to the chagrin of my fellow players. I don't want to see combat go away but, again, it shouldn't always be the only option.

To The Moon is a puzzle game (it's 95% dialogue but there's no choices and there's puzzles occasionally so I'm saying puzzle). There's nothing RPG about it at all (minus the parody and that it was made in RPG Maker - which is irrelevant really). It shouldn't have been used as an example.

I see a lot of his point. People clamoring for RPGs without the combat are essentially begging for Adventure games. But I also remember the decline of proper RPGs in the style of Fallout and Baldur's Gate differently than he does. It wasn't people saying RPGs were too number crunchy or had too much combat, it was the rise, accessibility and profitability of Action RPGs like Diablo which slowly stole the oxygen away from more traditional RPGs. As well as MMOs which if anything were more combat focused.

But I do agree that combat is required to be considered a proper RPG. To insist otherwise goes down one of those nonsensical post-modern alleyways where anything can be anything and what's the point of defining genres at all.

I will say, RPGs don't necessarily need grindy combat, or expansive but often empty worlds full of repetitive travel. Even if those elements contribute to a sense of scope and adversity.

But, I do also have to agree with him at how obnoxious it is to have obvious posers trying to gain entry into fandoms, only to then spend most of their time complaining and trying to change things.
